name: Palovarotene
lead: Palovarotene is an oral retinoid that selectively activates retinoic acid receptor gamma (RAR-gamma). It is sold as Sohonos for fibrodysplasia ossificans progressiva (FOP), a rare genetic condition in which bone forms in muscles and connective tissue, gradually restricting movement and changing body shape.[1][2] Its relevance to appearance is as a member of the retinoid family that skin-focused readers know through tretinoin and isotretinoin, and as a drug that works to keep soft tissue free of unwanted bone growth, helping preserve posture, mobility and body contour in people with FOP.[1]

Palovarotene was first approved in Canada in January 2022 and has since been approved in the United States and Australia, while remaining unapproved in Europe at the time of the cited review.[1][2] It was previously studied for emphysema and for multiple hereditary exostoses, a condition in which benign bone growths form near the ends of long bones.[6][9]
It is a prescription drug used under specialist supervision, and its label carries boxed warnings for embryo-fetal toxicity and premature closure of growth plates in growing children.[12]

chain: Dampens BMP/SMAD signalling that drives bone formation in soft tissue
Fewer new heterotopic bone deposits, so body shape and movement are better preserved
angle.text: Palovarotene is not a cosmetic product. In people with FOP it is used to reduce new abnormal bone growth in muscle and soft tissue, which helps maintain posture, joint movement and the natural contour of the body. Skin-care readers may know the retinoid class from tretinoin; palovarotene is a selective, oral member of that family with a different medical purpose.

infobox: Prescription only; boxed warnings in the US label[12]

paras: The approved use is to reduce the formation of new heterotopic ossification (HO) in people with FOP, in adults and in children from roughly 8 years (females) or 10 years (males) in the Canadian approval.[1] FOP is caused by gain-of-function variants in the ACVR1/ALK2 gene, a bone morphogenetic protein receptor, and leads to progressive bone formation in sites such as the trunk and limbs.[4]
Palovarotene has also been tested in emphysema and in multiple hereditary exostosis, but is not approved for either.[6][9]

A randomized, placebo-controlled phase 2 trial (PIPAF) in FOP patients experiencing flare-ups evaluated palovarotene for preventing HO.[7] The open-label phase 3 MOVE trial followed with 107 participants and compared treated patients against untreated natural-history participants; its reports describe reduced new HO volume in treated patients.[14][15] Four-year data from MOVE have also been published.[11]
Expert reviewers describe the post hoc analyses as indicating modest benefit in limiting new HO, and note that limitations and open questions remain, including long-term risks and benefits.[2]

In the MO-Ped phase 2 trial in children with multiple hereditary exostosis, the trial was stopped over concerns about premature growth-plate closure; among the limited data collected, no significant difference in new osteochondromas was seen between groups.[6] A phase 2/3 trial in emphysema used the compound as an RAR-gamma agonist in a randomized design.[9]

The adverse-event profile is described as consistent with systemic retinoids.[6] The US label carries a boxed warning for embryo-fetal toxicity, with use contraindicated in pregnancy and conditional on pregnancy-prevention measures, and for premature epiphyseal (growth-plate) closure in growing children, for whom close monitoring is recommended.[12] In juvenile mice, palovarotene reduced HO but also produced marked skeletal toxicity.[18]

By binding RAR-gamma, palovarotene inhibits bone morphogenetic protein and SMAD 1/5/8 signalling, interfering with cartilage formation that precedes heterotopic bone and allowing normal muscle repair.[1][5] Laboratory work has also reported effects on the NF-kappa-B pathway.[13]
Phase 1 studies have examined food effects, drug interactions and exposure in Japanese and non-Japanese participants.[8][10]

Palovarotene was developed for emphysema in the 2000s and later repurposed for FOP; the FOP programme, run by Ipsen, passed through trial setbacks and regulatory delays before approval in Canada in 2022 and later in the US and Australia.[1][2][17]
Palovarotene is a rare-disease orphan therapy; it is discussed chiefly in FOP patient and clinical contexts, and reviews describe its approval as a milestone for the FOP community.[2]

timeline.event: Phase 2 PIPAF trial in FOP begins.[16]
First approval, in Canada, for FOP.[1]

card.summary: An oral selective retinoid that limits abnormal bone growth in soft tissue in FOP, helping preserve mobility and body shape.
card.note: Prescription-only rare-disease drug with boxed warnings for pregnancy and children's growth plates.

quick.overview:
Palovarotene (Sohonos) is an oral retinoid approved for fibrodysplasia ossificans progressiva, a rare condition where bone grows in muscle and soft tissue.

By limiting new bone deposits it helps keep movement, posture and body contour from being progressively restricted. It is related to the retinoids used in skin care but is a specialist medicine.
quick.mechanism: It selectively activates RAR-gamma, which dampens BMP/SMAD signalling that drives cartilage and bone formation in injured muscle.
quick.risks: Boxed warnings cover birth defects and premature growth-plate closure in children. Other effects resemble those of systemic retinoids. It is prescription only.
